newsitem.title: UK: Fixed rate mortgages may blunt UK monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: Fixed rate mortgages may blunt UK monetary policy.

text.p: An increasing trend towards fixed rate UK mortgages, instead of the more traditional and volatile floating rate home loan could hamper the Bank of England's ability to cool consumer demand through higher official rates, analysts say.
"The rise in the popularity of fixed rate deals is diminishing the impact of monetary policy, at least in the short term," said Ciaran Barr, Senior UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Anecdotal evidence suggests the vast majority of outstanding British mortgages are still on a variable rate basis but the current climate of rising official rates is persuading many borrowers to opt for the security of loans which are fixed for at least part of their duration.
Concrete figures on the current split in the stock of mortgages are unavailable but the Council of Mortgage Lenders estimated in 1994 that 21 percent of outstanding home loans were at a fixed rate.
In a study on the shift to fixed rate borrowing, Barr has tracked the information on mortgage flows since 1994 and estimates that the proportion of outstanding mortgages has now risen to 25 percent.
"This rise reflects the fact that fixed rates have accounted for almost 30 percent of gross flows from mid-1994 to mid-1997," he said.

Data from the British Bankers Association, which covers around 40 percent of existing British mortgages, shows gross fixed rate borrowing for home loans leapt to 45 percent in the second quarter of this year from 34 percent in the first quarter and compared to 25 percent in the second quarter of 1996.

The scurry for fixed rate mortgages, which do not move at the whim of changes in Britain's official interest rates, has been sparked by four 1/4 point official rate rises in as many months and talk of more to come, possibly in November.

Additionally, increased competition and low swap rates mean that mortgage lenders have been offering attractive fixed rates, with some five-year deals at more than one point below prevailing variable rates.

By historical standards, both Britain's official interest rates at 7.0 percent and 8.45 percent standard mortgage rates are still low but the rising trend has triggered memories of the late 1980s when mortgage rates soared to more than 15.0 percent as the government increased official rates to dampen demand.

"If we get a wholesale shift in mortgage borrowing it will ultimately blunt the interest rate instrument, as some borrowers seek to by-pass rises in interest rates," said HSBC UK economist Jonathan Loynes.
"But with so little data available, it is hard to get a clear picture of what is really happening but it seems as though the vast majority of borrowers are still going to be hit by higher rates."

The difficulty of getting a true picture of what is happening to the British mortgage market is down to a number of factors, not least of which is the wide variation in the lengths of time for which mortgages are fixed -- usually ranging from a few months to five years.

There is also the problem of working out whether borrowers have re-fixed or changed to variable rates at the end of the fixed rate term as well as the added complication that in the increasingly competitive mortgage world, lenders are reluctant to reveal too many details of their loan books.
But some of the recent rises in mortgage rates have increased the spread between official and mortgage rates as lenders which could bolster the Bank of England power over the consumer sector.
"Some of the recent 25 basis point rises in base rates have been followed by 35 basis point increases in mortgage rates," said NatWest Markets UK economist John O'Sullivan.

"The housing market has started to pick up and the lenders have withdrawn some of the cheaper offers simply because there was sufficient demand for mortgages. Increased competition means they are now more concerned about keeping their borrowers," he said.
He argued lenders were starting to concentrate on luring investors through higher deposit rates, at the expense of higher mortgage rates for borrowers.

"This is offsetting the impact of any move to a higher proportion of fixed rate borrowing. On balance a rate rise (official) means you are probably more getting more bang for your buck than you would be in a purely neutral environment."
